newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD-Japan stocks struggle, but outlook good.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Japan stocks struggle, but outlook good.

text.p: Japan stocks are likely to continue to correct in the coming week as investors adjust their positions ahead of the expiry of June futures and options at the end of the week, brokers said.
But bargain-hunting by foreign investors and pension funds was likely to occur in times of weakness and a heavy fall was unlikely, they added.
"The Nikkei average has been struggling to keep above 20,500 without much success and investors are beginning to think about reducing their longs," said a dealer at a second-tier brokerage.

On Friday, the 225-share Nikkei average finished at 20,485.75, down 2.40 points, or 0.01 percent. Over the week it gained more than 400 points. It also achieved a new closing high for the calendar year, climbing to 20,611.56 during the week before falling on profit-taking.

"The rollover of futures contracts was a little late in starting and institutional investors are hoping that there will be a chance to bargain-hunt at the settlement on Friday," said Kunihiro Hatae, Tokyo Securities general manager.

Despite a possible spot of weakness brought on by expiry-related activity and technical factors following a rise of nearly eight percent by the Nikkei average in May, market sources said stocks were generally looking upward.

"U.S. stocks have been rising steadily and investors are getting a bit cautious, but Japanese stocks which have been left behind are a good buy and interest from foreign investors is very keen," said Keiko Kondo, a Merrill Lynch strategist.
In May, foreign investors bought 3.71 trillion yen worth of Japanese stocks on the Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya stock exchanges, the largest amount ever.
Kondo added that the market was just starting to react to corporate profit forecasts for the year to 1998 ending March.
Wako Research Institute said earlier it saw Japanese firms' profits rising 10.4 percent in 1997/98.
"There was much pessimism about the health of the economy in recent months, but the outlook is not so bad and investors could be a little more confident," Kondo added.
Yasuo Ueki, Nikko Securities general manager, said turnover held the key to gains and trade totalling 400 to 500 million shares was needed for the Nikkei benchmark to poke above the 21,000 barrier.
Trade had fallen to below 400 million in recent sessions.

Market participants will keep an eye out for further developments in the scandal involving Nomura Securities Co Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB), after the arrest on Thursday of DKB officials, brokers said.
The four officials were suspected of violating the Commercial Code by extending uncollateralised loans to the racketeer involved in the Nomura scandal.
"The market is in the process of digesting the effect of the scandal on the bank's business and the possible punitive measures," a broker at a major brokerage said.
